title: Demonstration of a Structured Agentic Workflow for Applied Quantum Computing Research
authors: Dikshant Dulal, Maxence Grandadam, Maciej Koch-Janusz, Mykola Maksymenko
abstract: Quantum hardware advances now make it practical to explore quantum approaches to scientific problems. Applied quantum computing research sits at the intersection of domain knowledge, algorithms, theoretical physics, device physics, and quantum and classical computational methods. The breadth of expertise required and the inherent project complexity challenge not only any individual researcher, but also generic AI systems. Here, we introduce the Quantum Agentic Operating System (QAOS), a structured agentic research system designed to address this challenge for quantum and computational R&D projects. QAOS is built around a nonlinear workflow graph of heterogeneous multi-agent nodes, with a controlled flow of context and computational resources. It decomposes a complex research project into sandboxed multi-agent tasks executed under constraints from the project graph, task-relevant methodologies, and necessary verification steps. We demonstrate QAOS on a quantum chemistry prototyping task, in which it is asked to set up a minimal model for a proton-transfer problem and to implement its solution using sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), together with classical reference methods such as FCI (exact diagonalization) and density functional theory (DFT). We compare the QAOS solution to those obtained with baseline agents (Claude Sonnet 5 with the Claude Code harness). In contrast to QAOS, the baseline agents silently ignore explicit instructions, and the runs show large variability.
summary: This paper introduces the Quantum Agentic Operating System (QAOS), a structured framework designed to manage the complexity of applied quantum computing research. It demonstrates QAOS by successfully calculating the proton transfer barrier for a model system, achieving results consistent with exact quantum chemistry benchmarks. The work highlights that structured, verifiable workflows are crucial for reliable quantum R&D, far surpassing the capabilities of unconstrained AI agents.
main_problem: To address the complexity of applied quantum computing research, the authors introduce a structured agentic workflow system.
main_result: The proposed Quantum Agentic Operating System (QAOS) successfully guides a quantum chemistry calculation, yielding results consistent with high-level theory (FCI) and significantly outperforming baseline, unstructured LLM attempts.
method: The core methodology is the QAOS, a structured, multi-agent workflow graph that decomposes complex research into sandboxed, verifiable tasks, contrasting with simple, single-prompt agent execution.
model_or_system: The demonstration uses the Zundel cation ($	ext{H}_5	ext{O}^+$) as a minimal model for proton transfer, requiring the calculation of the electronic ground-state energy via various methods.
key_observables: The energy barrier for proton transfer ($\Delta E_{	ext{barrier}}$) along the reaction coordinate ($\delta$).
important_parameters: Fixed inter-oxygen distance ($d = 2.9 	ext{ Å}$); minimal basis set (STO-3G); 20 electrons in 15 orbitals.
main_assumptions: The calculation is performed within the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, and the authors deliberately avoid active-space approximations for direct solver comparison.
figures_summary: Figure 2 compares potential-energy profiles for proton transfer using different electronic structure methods (SQD vs. exact FCI), showing the superior accuracy and consistency of the QAOS-guided approach compared to baseline LLM attempts.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the QAOS framework, demonstrates its application to a quantum chemistry prototyping task (proton transfer), compares its structured output against baseline agents, and validates the process using established quantum chemistry benchmarks.
why_interesting: The paper's focus on structuring the *process* of quantum algorithm development—managing context, enforcing constraints, and verifying steps—is highly relevant for researchers building complex quantum simulation pipelines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic view of the Quantum Agentic OS workflow used in this demonstration. Research and evidence stages (dark) generate a formalization, define a build protocol, and specify reference results to reproduce, which are human-approved. Test-driven implementation converts the protocol into immutable tests before coding. The implementation nodes (light) are guarded at each interface by the tests. Execution validates the interfaces and the run record, and a failed check returns work to the relevant upstream stage. Node labels and arrows remain legible in grayscale.

Figure 2: Left: Potential-energy profiles produced by the QAOS-guided protocol. FCI is exact within the STO-3G space; the quantum SQD method recovers the energy barrier to within 20 meV. Right: Five baseline FCI attempts using the standard Claude Code harness with the same Sonnet 5 model as QAOS. The baseline agents demonstrated large variability, breaking the brief by choosing different electronic subspaces and geometries, committing critical mistakes before even reaching the quantum algorithm stage. Legend labels identify each method for color and grayscale print.

Figure 3: Project graph for the proton-transfer demonstration as shown in the Quantum Agentic OS interface. Each node is a multi-agent module. Edges show the controlled flow of context used to assemble the experiment.

Figure 3 shows the project graph of nodes for the proton-transfer demonstration, as displayed in the Quantum Agentic OS interface. As in Section 2, each node is a multi-agent module in itself (or a local input folder attached to the graph). Edges indicate which completed outputs become available as context to later stages. Figure 1 is the schematic of the same organization. This appendix figure is the concrete graph used for the case study.

Figure 4: Geometry used for the proton-transfer scan. The oxygen–oxygen separation is fixed to 2.9 Å, and the shared proton is displaced along the O–O axis according to the reaction coordinate δ. The symmetric configuration lies near the center of the scan, while displacement toward either oxygen produces the two proton-localized sides of the potential-energy profile. We overlay a schematic of the potential energy as a function of δ, not to scale.
